Why NoSQL?The four NoSQL families

NoSQL is not one thing: four data models that are not tables

Key-Value StoreCore idea

The simplest of the four: a key, and whatever bytes you put under it

Key-Value StoreExample: user records

The key-value model is the simplest NoSQL model: data is stored as key-value pairs. It works well for applications that need fast lookups by a unique key.
For a user management system, user data can be stored as key-value pairs where the key is the UserID and the value is the associated user information.
Key: 1
Value: { "name": "John", "email": "john@email.com", "age": 28 }

Key: 2
Value: { "name": "Mike", "email": "mike@email.com", "age": 31 }
Very efficient for simple lookups, but no complex querying or relationships between data.

Key-Value StoreData model and operations

  • Data model: (key, value) pairs
    • Key = string/integer, unique for the entire data
    • Value = can be anything (very complex object)
  • Operations
    • get(key), put(key, value)
    • Operations on value not supported
      • user writes their own code for those

Key-Value StoreExamples: the same lookup pattern serves caches and persistent stores

Product / serviceTypical role
Redis / Redis CloudSessions, caches, counters, rate limits
Valkey / Amazon ElastiCacheManaged caching and sessions
MemcachedSimple in-memory cache
Amazon DynamoDBPersistent key-value and document data at scale
Choose by role and guarantees: a cache and a system of record differ

Wide-Column StoreCore idea

Looks like a table, but every row may have its own set of columns

Wide-Column StoreRows with their own columns

In the column-family model, data is organized into rows and columns, but unlike the relational model, each row can have a variable number of columns. It is optimized for fast querying and large-scale distributed storage.
Example: a user activity tracking system that stores the actions users take on a website, such as page views and purchases. Each user has a unique UserID, and their activity is stored in a column family.
Column Family: UserActivity
Row Key (UserID)Page1Page2Purchase1Purchase2
1Viewed: Home PageViewed: ProductsProduct: Laptop ($1200)Product: Phone ($800)
2Viewed: Home PageViewed: Contact UsProduct: TV ($1500)
3Viewed: Home PageProduct: Camera ($600)

Wide-Column StoreExample: user activity

Row Key (UserID): the unique identifier for each user.
Page1, Page2, Purchase1, Purchase2: columns representing the user’s activity, which can vary from row to row.
  • Each user (row) can have a variable number of columns, and different users may have different activities stored
  • In Bigtable-style models, column families are declared; column qualifiers can be added per row
  • High write throughput and distributed storage, but it doesn’t enforce strict relationships like the relational model

Wide-Column StoreData model: BigTable and HBase

  • Also called wide-column stores
  • Based on Google’s BigTable
  • HBase is an open source implementation of BigTable
  • Data model:
    • Variant 1: key = rowID, value = record
    • Variant 2: key = (rowID, columnID), value = field
      • Or multiple columnIDs in the key

Wide-Column StoreExamples: designed for many writes and key-range reads

Product / serviceWhat to recognize
Apache CassandraPartition key + ordered rows (CQL declares its columns)
Google Cloud BigtableRow keys + sparse cells; HBase is its open-source relative
ScyllaDB CloudManaged Cassandra-compatible service
Same family, different concrete models: check the product’s key model

Graph StoreCore idea

Nodes and edges are the data; following an edge replaces a join

Graph StoreEdges instead of foreign keys

The same five entities: edges on the left, foreign keys and joins on the right

Graph StoreProperty graphs

A property graph: both nodes and edges carry attributes

Graph StoreWhen a graph fits

Graph databases represent relationships as edges and offer traversal queries. Relational databases can use an edge table with a relationship-type column. The better fit depends on the traversal pattern and workload.
Friendship as a table: two-hop paths use two copies of the edge table

Graph StoreCypher: nodes and edges

CREATE (p1:Person {name: 'Harry'}), (p2:Person {name: 'Anna'})
CREATE (p1)-[r:MARRIED_TO]->(p2)
RETURN p1, r, p2;
Two nodes and one directed edge, written as a pattern rather than as rows

Graph StoreRecursive queries: SQL and Cypher

With breadth-first and depth-first search it is possible to obtain the descendants in a specific order. Here are the SQL and Cypher queries to find all descendants of Thurimbert:
WITH RECURSIVE descendants AS (
  SELECT person FROM tree
  WHERE  parent = 'Thurimbert'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT t.person
  FROM   descendants d, tree t
  WHERE  t.parent = d.person
)
SELECT * FROM descendants;
MATCH path = (n:Person {name: 'Thurimbert'})-[*]->(m)
RETURN m;
Any depth: SQL recurses one join per level, Cypher writes one path pattern

Graph StoreExamples: chosen when paths of unknown depth are the common question

Product / serviceModel and query style
Neo4j / AuraDBProperty graph, Cypher (managed: AuraDB)
Amazon NeptuneProperty graph and RDF; openCypher, Gremlin, SPARQL
MemgraphIn-memory property graph, Cypher
A graph store fits multi-hop questions; a fixed-depth join may not need one

Document StoreCore idea

A key-value store whose values have structure the store can read

Document StoreValues with structure

  • In key-value stores, the value is often a very complex object
    • Key = 'GizmoWorks', Value = [all products of that company]
  • Better: value to be structured data
    • JSON or Protobuf or XML
    • Called a “document” but it’s just data
We will discuss JSON

Document StoreExamples: one document holds what the application reads together

DataWhy a document fitsExample product / service
Product catalogFields vary by productMongoDB / Atlas
User profileRelated fields are read togetherMongoDB / Atlas, Couchbase
Web and mobile app recordsObjects in the shape the app readsCloud Firestore
JSON inside a relational DBMixed with tables and SQLPostgreSQL jsonb, SQLite JSON
JSON data can also live inside a SQL database

JSON Overview

  • JavaScript Object Notation = lightweight text-based open standard designed for human-readable data interchange. Interfaces in C, C++, Java, Python, Perl, etc.
  • The filename extension is .json.
We will emphasize JSON as semi-structured data

JSON Syntax

{ "book": [
    { "id": "01",
      "language": "Java",
      "author": "H. Javeson",
      "year": 2015
    },
    { "id": "07",
      "language": "C++",
      "edition": "second",
      "author": "E. Sepp",
      "price": 22.25
    }
  ]
}

JSON vs Relational

  • Relational data model
    • Rigid flat structure (tables)
    • Schema must be fixed in advance
    • Storage encoding is a separate design choice
    • Query language based on Relational Algebra
  • Semistructured data model / JSON
    • Flexible, nested structure (trees)
    • Does not require predefined schema (“self-describing”)
    • JSON text is an interchange format; stores may use binary encodings
    • Queries via MQL, SQL/JSON, and other languages

JSON Types

  • Primitive: number, string, Boolean, null
  • Object: collection of name-value pairs:
    • {"name1": value1, "name2": value2, …}
    • “name” is also called a “key”
  • Array: ordered list of values:
    • [obj1, obj2, obj3, ...]

Avoid Using Duplicate Keys

The standard allows them, but many implementations don’t
{ "id": "07",
  "title": "Databases",
  "author": "Garcia-Molina",
  "author": "Ullman",same key again
  "author": "Widom"
}
→
Use an ordered list instead
{ "id": "07",
  "title": "Databases",
  "author": ["Garcia-Molina",one key, an array
             "Ullman",
             "Widom"]
}

JSON Semantics: A Tree!

{"person":
  [ {"name": "Mary",
     "address":
       {"street": "Maple",
        "no": 345,
        "city": "SF"}},
    {"name": "John",
     "address": "Thailand",
     "phone": 23456}
  ]
}
Every value sits at the end of one path from the root

JSON Semantics: A Tree!

{"person":
  [ {"name": "Mary",
     "address":
       {"street": "Maple",
        "no": 345,
        "city": "SF"}},
    {"name": "John",
     "address": "Thailand",
     "phone": 23456}
  ]
}
Recall: arrays are ordered in JSON!
Array positions 0 and 1 label edges too, so arrays keep their order; relations do not

Semi-Structured Data

  • JSON is self-describing
  • Schema elements become part of the data
    • Relational schema: person(name, phone)
    • In JSON "person", "name", "phone" are part of the data, and are repeated many times
  • ⇒ JSON is more flexible
    • Schema can change per tuple

Storing JSON in RDBMS

  • Using JSON as a data type provided by RDBMSs
    • Declare a column that contains either json or jsonb (binary)
      • CREATE TABLE people (person json)   [or jsonb for binary]
    • In our previous example, we will have one row per person
      • i.e., a row corresponding to that person’s attributes
    • Queries now mix relational and semi-structured syntax
      • SELECT * FROM people WHERE person @> '{"name": "Mary"}';
  • Translate JSON documents into relations

A table is an array of objects: one object per row, one key per column

Mapping Semi-Structured Data to RelationsMissing attributes

  • Missing attributes:
{"person":
  [{"name": "John", "phone": 1234},

namephone
John1234

Mapping Semi-Structured Data to RelationsRepeated attributes

  • Repeated attributes
{"person":
  [{"name": "John", "phone": 1234},
   {"name": "Mary", "phone": [1234, 5678]}]   // two phones!
}
  • Not in one scalar phone column:
namephone
Mary23453456???

Mapping Semi-Structured Data to RelationsAttributes with mixed types

  • Attributes with different types in different objects
{"person":
  [{"name": "Sue", "phone": 3456},
   {"name": {"first": "John", "last": "Smith"},   // structured name!
    "phone": 2345}]
}
  • Nested collections
  • Heterogeneous collections
  • These are difficult to represent in the relational model

Answer: JSON Inside a SQL Table

SELECT p.id, p.person ->> '$.name' AS name, j.value AS phone
FROM   people p, json_each(p.person, '$.phone') j;
idnamephone
1John1234
2Mary1234
2Mary5678
4{"first":"John","last":"Smith"}2345
json_each turns the phone array into rows: Mary twice, Joe not at all. The relational answer to a repeated attribute is a second table, built here on the fly.
A repeated attribute becomes one row per value: the join is back

Discussion: Why Semi-Structured Data?

  • Semi-structured data works well as data exchange formats
    • i.e., exchanging data between different apps
    • Examples: XML, JSON, Protobuf (protocol buffers)
  • Increasingly, systems use them as a data model for DBs:
    • SQL Server supports XML-valued relations
    • CouchBase, MongoDB, Snowflake: JSON
    • Dremel (BigQuery): Protobuf

Semi-Structured Data Model

  • Nested formats: JSON, XML; Protobuf requires a message schema
  • Data model = Tree
  • Query language take non first normal form into account as we will see
    • Various “extra” constructs introduced as a result
      • Nesting & Unnesting, strict aggregates, splitting

Why NoSQL? – Data Model

First answer: the data is not shaped like a table

Why NoSQL? – Schema-lessSQL: schema first

Let’s take the example of a user management system. In SQL, we first define the structure (schema) of the Users and Orders tables before adding data.
CREATE TABLE Users (
  UserID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name   VARCHAR(100),
  Email  VARCHAR(100),
  Age    INT
);
CREATE TABLE Orders (
  OrderID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  UserID  INT,
  Product VARCHAR(100),
  Price   DECIMAL(10, 2),
  FOREIGN KEY (UserID) REFERENCES Users(UserID)
);

Why NoSQL? – Schema-lessDocuments: mixed shapes

Document databases can allow mixed record shapes. Adding a field need not rewrite every document, but readers, validation rules, and old records may still need migration.
Example: User and Orders in a Document Database (e.g., MongoDB)
In a document-based NoSQL database, you store user and order data in a single document.
{
  "_id": 1,
  "name": "John",
  "email": "john@email.com",
  "age": 28,
  "orders": [orders live inside the user
    { "orderId": 101,
      "product": "Laptop",
      "price": 1200 },
    { "orderId": 104,
      "product": "Smartphone",
      "price": 800 }
  ]
}

Why NoSQL? – ScalabilityScale up

A single-server system can scale vertically (also known as scale-up).
This means improving performance and capacity by adding more power (e.g., CPU, RAM, or storage) to a single server.
Scale up: the same server, made bigger

Why NoSQL? – ScalabilityScale out

Distributed SQL and many NoSQL systems scale horizontally (also known as scale-out).
This means increasing capacity by adding more servers or nodes to a distributed system.
Scale out: more servers, and the data must be split among them

Asynchronous Leader–Follower ReplicationFollowers replay the leader’s log asynchronously, so a follower read can return an older value

A read from the lagging follower returns the old value

CAP TheoremA partition forces a choice: block some operations, or answer without a consistency guarantee

Without a partition, replication still trades latency against consistency
During a partition, a system cannot guarantee both linearizable operations and availability

SQL vs NoSQLACID

SQL databases are known for their robust support of ACID transactions (Lecture 6).
  • Atomicity: a transaction is a single, indivisible unit. All of its operations succeed, or none are applied.
  • Consistency: a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, keeping constraints, triggers and types intact.
  • Isolation: the isolation level defines which interactions concurrent transactions may observe.
  • Durability: once committed, the result survives a crash.
This makes SQL databases ideal where data integrity and consistency are critical, such as financial systems.

SQL vs NoSQLBASE

Some distributed systems favor availability with eventual consistency, often described as BASE:
  • Basically Available: aim to keep serving requests during failures; success is not unconditional.
  • Soft state: replicas may differ while updates propagate.
  • Eventually consistent: replicas converge once writes stop and communication and reconciliation resume.
NoSQL does not imply BASE. MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions; guarantees depend on the product and configuration.

Case study: Amazon DynamoDynamo prioritized cart writes during failures and let the application reconcile conflicting versions

Two versions merged by union: a deleted item can come back

SQL vs NoSQLGuarantees depend on the product, the operation and the settings

Product / operationWhat is supported
MongoDB multi-document transactionsAtomic changes across several documents
DynamoDB table and LSI readsStrongly consistent reads can be requested
DynamoDB global secondary index readsEventually consistent only
Cassandra writes and readsTunable: how many replicas must answer
A database family is not a consistency setting: check the product, the operation and the configuration
Model, transaction scope and replica reads are three separate questions

Discussion: Which Store Would You Try?Start with the question, then choose a candidate

NeedMain question
Login sessionsRetrieve a user by session ID
Device readingsRead one device over a time range
Suspicious account linksFollow shared devices and payment links
Product catalogQuery products with different fields
For each row: one candidate family and one caveat to check before choosing

Answer: Which Store Would You Try?Name the question first; the product comes last

NeedCandidateCheck before choosing
SessionsKey-valueExpiry and persistence
Device readingsWide-columnKey distribution and group size
Account linksGraphPath depth and candidate count
CatalogDocumentIndexes and shared updates
These are starting candidates, not exclusive answers: SQL and SQL with JSON remain valid for all four

Takeaway: NoSQL I

1NoSQL is four data models, not one technology: key-value, wide-column, graph, document, each with products chosen by role.
2JSON is a tree that describes itself: keys travel with the data, arrays keep their order, and a repeated attribute needs a second table on the way into a relation.
3The reasons are data model, schema-less writes and scale-out; scale-out brings lagging replicas, so check each product’s consistency and transaction guarantees.
